title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E449 proves results on the residues of geometric progressions 1, a, a^2, … modulo a prime P. On the previous page (§34) Euler counts the 'casus proprii' of x^n − 1, i.e. the roots that satisfy no lower formula x^d − 1 with d|n. He does this by inclusion–exclusion over the divisors of n and gets n∏(1−1/p) = φ(n). In modern terms these are the primitive n-th roots of unity.

§35 (Coroll. 1) carries this over to residues mod P. For n = P−1, x^{P−1} − 1 ≡ 0 has all P−1 nonzero residues as roots, by Fermat. Euler then asserts that once the roots shared with lower formulae are removed, the remaining 'proper' roots are all real, i.e. exist mod P.

§36 (Coroll. 2), this page: there always exist numbers a < P that are proper roots of x^{P−1} − 1. Such an a satisfies no lower x^d − 1. In modern terms: there exist elements of multiplicative order exactly P−1 mod P. Euler's count implies there are φ(P−1) of them.

§37 (Scholion): the abstract counting is needed for the following proofs. The key fact to prove is that for every prime P some geometric progression 1, a, a^2, … gives a 'complete' residue series, containing every number below P before the residues repeat. This is the existence of a primitive root. Euler makes three further remarks:
- Many would think the fact needs no proof, because such a are easily found for small primes.
- For larger primes 'the reason for doubt seems to decrease continually', a heuristic remark.
- The fact nevertheless requires proof, because it fails for composite moduli.

§38 (Theorema, statement begun here): for every prime P a primitive root a exists. The proof on the next page combines three steps:
- If a^n ≡ 1 with n < P−1, then n divides P−1 (§21).
- §34 supplies an a whose lowest power ≡ 1 is a^{P−1}.
- The P−1 residues before the first return to 1 are therefore distinct, so the series is complete.
errors: Gap, not a false statement: the existence of 'proper cases' mod P (Coroll. 1–2) is inferred from a count, φ(n), that is valid for complex roots of unity. To transfer it to residues mod P one needs that x^d − 1 has exactly d roots mod P for every d | P−1. That follows from Lagrange's theorem (a polynomial has at most deg roots mod p) together with x^d − 1 dividing the fully split x^{P−1} − 1. Euler does not supply this justification on this page or the next. Gauss (Disquisitiones, art. 56) judged Euler's demonstration of primitive roots deficient on essentially this point.

Statement remark: the Scholion's claim that the property fails for 'divisores non-primi' is true in general (e.g. 8, 12, 15) but not universally. Primitive roots exist for 4, p^k and 2p^k, a refinement Euler does not mention.

ideas.what: Existence of elements of exact order P−1 mod a prime P (complete residue series of a geometric progression)
ideas.modern_name: Existence of primitive roots modulo a prime
ideas.usually_credited_to: Stated by Lambert (1769); attempted proof by Euler in E449 (1774); first rigorous proofs by Legendre (1785) and Gauss (Disquisitiones, 1801)
ideas.where_published: E449, Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petrop. 18 (1774); the term 'radix primitiva' appears here in E449

ideas.what: Number of 'proper cases' of x^{P−1} − 1 equals φ(P−1), hence the number of primitive roots
ideas.modern_name: Count of primitive roots = φ(p−1); primitive roots of unity counted by Euler's totient

ideas.what: Observation that complete residue series fail for composite moduli, so the prime case needs proof
ideas.modern_name: Non-cyclicity of (Z/nZ)^* for most composite n
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss (full classification of moduli with primitive roots, Disq. arts. 82–92)

deep.surprise_reason: This page is the well-known statement of Euler's primitive-root theorem and its motivation. The proof's gap and its history (Lambert, Euler, Legendre, Gauss) are thoroughly documented, e.g. by Gauss himself and in Sandifer's 'How Euler Did It' columns. The heuristic remark about doubt decreasing for larger primes is a minor curiosity, not a missed result.
transcription_corrections: Running head appears as 'PER NVNEROS PRIMOS' in the print, evidently a misprint for 'NVMEROS'; the transcription faithfully reproduces it.
Signature mark at foot: 'N 2' with catchwords '1, a,' — correctly transcribed.
